cards.body: This week spanned two worlds: the final golden days of Japan — Shinjuku, the Kyoto train, a first-class departure — and full submersion into Bora Bora's lagoon. The emotional shift was real: where February ended with 'can't help but feel like I'm not moving quick enough,' this week's journals read 'really really great day' and 'so thankful to be here.' The anxiety is gone. The gratitude is the whole story.
cards.quote: Very grateful for the time we had in Japan. It was incredible and I cannot wait to be back.
cards.headline: Japan concluded in gratitude. Bora Bora answered with floaties and presence.

moments.body: Michelin-star dinner, matcha, Shibuya Crossing, an arcade, onsen, and sake with a high-ranking Japanese air defense officer in Golden Gai — all in one day. Golden Gai's 200-odd tiny bars, each seating maybe six people, are one of Tokyo's great social accidents: strangers become friends in minutes. This was that kind of night. You called it 'like a perfect day in Tokyo' — and the detail density of that journal entry suggests you meant it literally.
moments.title: The Perfect Tokyo Day

moments.body: A first-class flight from Japan to French Polynesia is a rare hinge moment — one extraordinary chapter closing as another begins mid-air. You landed in Bora Bora with the lagoon's improbable turquoise waiting, and wrote with pure relief: 'Cannot wait for what Bora Bora has to offer.' The overwater bungalows of the Society Islands sit above water so clear you can watch fish from your deck. After ten days of Tokyo and Kyoto sensory overload, the stillness hits differently.
moments.title: Japan Closes, Bora Bora Opens

moments.body: Tennis with Dave, a run, weights, poolside cabana booked, alcohol avoided, and four Gremly todos shipped — all framed as a single 'great day' rather than a series of trade-offs. The long sleep clearly helped: 'Felt very very refreshed this morning.' This is the week's clearest expression of how you operate at your best: fitness, partnership, creative work, and discipline as one integrated thing, not competing demands.

spotlight.title: Work follows you — then you notice
spotlight.takeaway: The pattern isn't that you can't stop working — it's that naming the tension out loud is what actually releases it. The March 12 journal acted as a reset switch, and March 13 was the result.
spotlight.evidence_trail: March 2 (Tokyo, first day of PTO): worked through the morning to 'make sure the handover was in a good place.' March 8-9 (Bora Bora, day 2-3): completed 4 Gremly todos in 48 hours — Daily Context Object Integration, Fed Metaphor Exploration, DCO User Onboarding, DCO Implementation. March 13: completed 'Work Plan for Hawaii' before arriving there. That's three separate destinations where work was the first thing you reached for. Then March 12 — day 6 of Bora Bora — a different entry: 'Realizing that even though I love Gremly work, I need to step back sometimes and just enjoy him.' The day after that journal entry, March 13, produced your most purely present entry of the entire trip: 'Really really great day. So thankful to be here.'

research_context.body: Psychological research on 'cognitive offloading' suggests that externalizing a competing priority — writing it down, speaking it aloud — reduces its pull on working memory. For people who find meaning in their work (and your profile suggests Gremly is genuinely identity-adjacent, not just a job), the urge to engage doesn't disappear on vacation; it just needs a conscious redirect. The March 12 journal entry did exactly that: it acknowledged the pull, named the higher priority, and freed up presence. The fact that your best day followed immediately isn't coincidence.
research_context.title: Why naming it works

cards.body: The month's arc is clean: February was the sprint, the ship, the exhaustion. The Feb 27 journal — 'I need this holiday' — was the hinge. March became something different: slower, warmer, more present. The anxiety that defined the pre-launch weeks didn't follow you to Japan. What followed you instead was your work — but even that softened by Bora Bora. The month ends with a half marathon two weeks away and Hawaii beginning. That's a different kind of momentum.
cards.headline: A launch sprint became a honeymoon, and the anxiety went with it.

thread_arcs.arc: February opened with pre-launch compression — 14 tasks closed in a single day before TestFlight shipped Feb 26 — then shifted to vacation-integrated DCO iteration in Bora Bora, with four completions in 48 hours and genuine excitement replacing the 'not moving quick enough' anxiety.
Started the month as a background presence during the work sprint, became the explicit anchor of meaning by March 12 when you chose him over Gremly mid-vacation.
Survived the LA-Tulum-Tokyo-Bora Bora travel gauntlet intact — 133% habit completion across three weeks — and is now two weeks from its milestone.

The January 1 commitment met its first real test in the honeymoon's social and celebratory context, finishing the month at 29% completion — still active, but the gap between intention and execution is widening.
